1. Union–State Resource Sharing — Meaning and Need

  • India has a federal fiscal system in which the Union and State Governments have different constitutional responsibilities.
  • Revenue-raising powers and expenditure responsibilities are not distributed equally between the two levels.
  • Constitutional and institutional mechanisms are therefore needed to transfer resources and maintain fiscal balance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Federalism → Revenue Powers + Expenditure Responsibilities + Transfers

2. State Expenditure Responsibilities

States have major expenditure responsibilities in:

  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Agriculture.
  • Drinking water.
  • Sanitation.
  • Welfare.
  • Police.
  • Public services.
  • Local infrastructure.
  • Adequate resource sharing is necessary because States directly provide many day-to-day public services.

3. Fiscal Federalism — Core Meaning

  • Fiscal federalism refers to the constitutional and institutional division of revenue powers, expenditure responsibilities and financial transfers among different levels of government.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Federalism → Who Raises + Who Spends + Who Transfers

4. Part XII — Union–State Financial Relations

  • Part XII of the Constitution contains major provisions dealing with Union–State financial relations.
  • Important tax-assignment, tax-sharing, grant and Finance Commission provisions fall within this constitutional framework.

5. High-Yield Constitutional Article Chain

  • Article 268 → Union levy, State collection and appropriation.
  • Article 269 → Union levy and collection, proceeds assigned to States.
  • Article 269A → Inter-State GST.
  • Article 270 → Divisible pool.
  • Article 271 → Union surcharge.
  • Article 275 → Grants-in-aid.
  • Article 279A → GST Council.
  • Article 280 → Finance Commission.
  • Article 281 → Finance Commission recommendations before Parliament.
  • Article 282 → Grants for public purposes.
📌 Must-Memorise

268 → 269 → 269A → 270 → 271 → 275 → 279A → 280 → 281 → 282

6. Article 246A — GST Legislative Powers

  • Article 246A gives Parliament and State Legislatures power to make laws regarding GST.
  • Parliament has exclusive power regarding GST on supplies occurring in inter-State trade or commerce.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 246A → GST Law-Making Power

7. Article 268 — Union Levy, State Collection

  • Article 268 deals with specified duties levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by States.
  • Where such duties are leviable within a State, the State collects them.
  • The proceeds attributable to that State are appropriated by it.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 268 → Union Levies, State Collects and Keeps

8. Article 269 — Union Levy and Collection, State Assignment

  • Article 269 covers specified taxes levied and collected by the Union.
  • Their proceeds are assigned to States according to constitutional rules.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 269 → Union Levies + Union Collects + States Receive Proceeds

9. Article 268 vs Article 269

  • Article 268 → Union levies, State collects and appropriates.
  • Article 269 → Union levies and collects, proceeds assigned to States.
📌 Must-Memorise

268 → State Collects

269 → Union Collects

10. Article 269A — Inter-State GST

  • GST on inter-State supplies is governed by Article 269A.
  • It is levied and collected by the Government of India.
  • Proceeds are apportioned between the Union and States according to law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 269A → Inter-State GST

11. IGST — Meaning

  • GST on inter-State supplies is commonly called Integrated Goods and Services Tax, or IGST.
📌 Must-Memorise

IGST → Inter-State GST

12. Article 269A vs Article 279A

  • Article 269A → Inter-State GST levy, collection and apportionment.
  • Article 279A → GST Council.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

269A ≠ 279A

13. Article 270 — Divisible Pool

  • Article 270 provides the constitutional basis for distribution of shareable Union taxes between the Union and States.
  • The shareable collection of Union taxes is commonly called the divisible pool.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 270 → Divisible Pool

14. Divisible Pool — Meaning

  • The divisible pool consists of constitutionally shareable Union tax proceeds.
  • The Finance Commission recommends the States' collective share.
  • That collective share is then distributed among individual States through the horizontal formula.

15. Divisible Pool — Major Exclusions

The ordinary divisible-pool framework excludes specified collections such as:

  • Taxes under Article 268.
  • Taxes under Article 269.
  • GST under Article 269A.
  • Surcharges under Article 271.
  • Specific-purpose cesses.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Divisible Pool ≠ Gross Union Tax Revenue

16. Net Proceeds — Important Concept

  • Tax devolution is based on relevant net proceeds rather than merely gross tax collections.
  • Applicable collection costs and constitutional exclusions affect the shareable amount.

17. Cess — Divisible-Pool Treatment

  • A cess is generally imposed for a specified purpose.
  • Specific-purpose cesses are excluded from the ordinary divisible pool under the constitutional framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cess → Generally Outside Ordinary Divisible Pool

18. Surcharge — Article 271

  • Article 271 allows Parliament to impose surcharges on specified taxes for Union purposes.
  • The proceeds accrue to the Union.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 271 → Surcharge → Union

19. Cess and Surcharge — Federal Significance

  • Cesses and surcharges are generally excluded from Finance Commission divisible-pool sharing.
  • Their increasing use can reduce the divisible pool relative to gross Union tax revenue.
  • Several States, including Tamil Nadu, have raised concerns regarding this issue.

20. 41% Share — Correct Base

  • The States' vertical share applies to the divisible pool.
  • It does not apply mechanically to every rupee of gross Union tax revenue.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

41% ≠ 41% of Gross Union Tax Revenue

21. Vertical Devolution — Meaning

  • Vertical devolution means distribution of the divisible pool between the Union and all States collectively.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vertical → Union vs States Collectively

22. Sixteenth Finance Commission — Vertical Share

According to the supplied source for 2026–31:

  • States collectively → 41% of divisible pool.
  • Union → 59% within the corresponding divisible-pool split.
📌 Must-Memorise

States 41% : Union 59%

23. Vertical Fiscal Imbalance

  • Vertical fiscal imbalance arises when revenue capacities and expenditure responsibilities differ between levels of government.
  • The Union has access to several broad tax bases.
  • States carry large responsibilities for public-service delivery.

24. Correcting Vertical Fiscal Imbalance

The main mechanisms include:

  • Tax devolution.
  • Grants.
  • Other constitutionally permitted fiscal transfers.

25. Horizontal Devolution — Meaning

  • Horizontal devolution means distribution of the States' collective share among individual States.
  • It answers how the States' 41% collective share is divided among the States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Horizontal → Among States

26. Vertical vs Horizontal Devolution

  • Vertical → How much goes to all States collectively.
  • Horizontal → How the collective State share is divided among individual States.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Vertical ≠ Among States

Horizontal ≠ Union vs States

27. Sixteenth Finance Commission — Horizontal Criteria

According to the supplied source:

  • 2011 Population → 17.5%.
  • Demographic Performance → 10%.
  • Area → 10%.
  • Forest → 10%.
  • Per-Capita GSDP Distance → 42.5%.
  • Contribution to GDP → 10%.
📌 Must-Memorise

17.5 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 42.5 + 10

28. Largest Horizontal Criterion

  • Per-capita GSDP distance carries the largest weight at 42.5%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Largest Criterion → GSDP Distance → 42.5%

29. Horizontal Formula — What Each Criterion Reflects

  • Population → Public-service needs.
  • Demographic Performance → Population-management performance.
  • Area → Administrative and infrastructure costs.
  • Forest → Ecological contributions and opportunity costs.
  • GSDP Distance → Fiscal-capacity equalisation.
  • GDP Contribution → Economic-performance consideration.

30. Fiscal Equalisation — Meaning

  • Fiscal equalisation seeks to reduce excessive differences in States' ability to provide comparable public services.
  • Lower-capacity States may receive relatively greater support through equalisation-oriented criteria.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Equalisation → Reduce Fiscal-Capacity Gaps

31. Equalisation Does Not Mean Equal Transfers

  • Fiscal equalisation does not mean every State receives exactly the same amount.
  • Transfers differ according to formula-based fiscal needs and other criteria.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Equalisation ≠ Equal Rupee Transfer

32. Horizontal Fiscal Imbalance

Horizontal fiscal imbalance arises because States differ in:

  • Population.
  • Per capita income.
  • Industrialisation.
  • Geography.
  • Forest cover.
  • Revenue capacity.
  • Infrastructure requirements.
  • Development needs.

33. Finance Commission — Article 280 Role

The Finance Commission recommends:

  • Vertical devolution.
  • Horizontal distribution.
  • Principles governing grants.
  • Measures to augment State Consolidated Funds for local bodies.
  • Other fiscal matters referred to it.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 280 → Finance Commission

34. Article 275 — Grants-in-Aid

  • Article 275 provides for grants-in-aid from the Consolidated Fund of India to States requiring assistance.
  • It also contains provisions connected with Scheduled Tribe welfare and Scheduled Areas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 275 → Grants + ST Welfare + Scheduled Areas

35. Article 275 vs Article 280

  • Article 275 → Grants-in-aid.
  • Article 280 → Finance Commission.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

275 ≠ 280

36. Article 282 — Public-Purpose Grants

  • Article 282 allows the Union or a State to make grants for any public purpose.
  • It provides constitutional flexibility for development-oriented transfers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 282 → Grant for Any Public Purpose

37. Finance Commission Transfers vs Other Transfers

  • Finance Commission transfers arise from recommendations under Article 280.
  • Other Union transfers may arise through schemes, grants and other constitutional or budgetary mechanisms.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

All Union Transfers ≠ Finance Commission Transfers

38. GST — Major Fiscal-Federal Reform

  • GST significantly changed India's indirect-tax structure.
  • It created a shared Union-State framework for taxation and decision-making.

39. GST Constitutional Chain

  • Article 246A → GST legislative powers.
  • Article 269A → Inter-State GST.
  • Article 279A → GST Council.
📌 Must-Memorise

246A → GST Laws

269A → Inter-State GST

279A → GST Council

40. GST Council — Cooperative Federalism

  • The GST Council provides an institutional forum for Union and State participation in GST-related decisions.
  • It is an important example of cooperative fiscal federalism.
📌 Must-Memorise

GST Council → Cooperative Fiscal Federalism

41. GST Council — Voting Structure

According to the constitutional voting arrangement:

  • Union Government → 1/3 of total weighted votes cast.
  • All States together → 2/3.
  • Decision threshold → At least 3/4 of weighted votes of members present and voting.
📌 Must-Memorise

Union → 1/3

States → 2/3

Decision → 3/4

42. State Public-Service Context

States require substantial resources because they directly finance and administer areas such as:

  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Agriculture.
  • Water.
  • Sanitation.
  • Welfare.
  • Law and order.

43. Tamil Nadu — Inter Se Share

According to the supplied source:

  • Tamil Nadu's inter se share in the States' collective divisible-pool portion → 4.097%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → 4.097%

44. Tamil Nadu — Correct Interpretation

The calculation occurs in two stages:

1. States collectively receive 41% of the divisible pool.

2. Tamil Nadu receives 4.097% of that collective States' share.

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tamil Nadu 4.097% ≠ 4.097% of Gross Union Tax Revenue

45. Tamil Nadu and Cess/Surcharge Concern

  • Tamil Nadu raised concerns about the effect of cesses and surcharges on the size of the divisible pool.
  • This reflects a wider Union-State debate over the shareable tax base.

46. Union Fiscal Responsibilities

The Union requires resources for:

  • Defence.
  • National infrastructure.
  • Debt servicing.
  • National programmes.
  • Union administration.

47. State Fiscal Responsibilities

  • States require large and predictable resources because they provide many essential public services directly to citizens.
  • Predictability of transfers is therefore important for State budgeting and planning.

48. Vertical Devolution — Policy Debate

  • One major fiscal-federal debate concerns the appropriate size of the collective State share.
  • Several States sought a higher share.
  • The Sixteenth Finance Commission retained 41% for the 2026–31 award period according to the supplied source.

49. Equity vs Contribution Debate

  • Lower-income States may emphasise development needs and equalisation.
  • Higher-income States may emphasise economic contribution and performance incentives.
  • Horizontal formulas therefore attempt to balance equity and performance.

50. Contribution to GDP — Performance Criterion

  • Contribution to GDP carries a 10% weight under the Sixteenth Finance Commission formula in the supplied source.
  • This introduces a direct economic-contribution element into horizontal distribution.

51. GSDP Distance — Strong Equalisation Weight

  • Per-capita GSDP distance carries 42.5%, much larger than the 10% contribution-to-GDP weight.
  • Equalisation therefore remains a major element of the horizontal formula.

52. Resource Sharing — Equity and Performance Balance

The formula combines:

  • Fiscal need.
  • Demographic considerations.
  • Geography.
  • Ecology.
  • Economic contribution.
  • Fiscal equalisation.

53. Predictability of Transfers

  • State Governments require predictable transfers for expenditure planning.
  • Uncertain transfers can complicate budgeting and public-service delivery.

54. Fiscal Discipline

  • Resource sharing must provide adequate funds while preserving overall fiscal responsibility.
  • Greater transfers alone do not eliminate the need for prudent revenue and expenditure management.

55. Union–State–Local Coordination

  • Many public services require coordination across Union, State and local levels.
  • Fiscal transfers therefore support not only State Governments but also local public-service systems.

56. Transfer Effectiveness

  • Resource sharing is not only about the amount of money transferred.
  • The ultimate objective is better public-service delivery and improved development outcomes.

57. Core Constitutional Resource-Sharing Chain

Tax Assignment

→ Divisible Pool

→ Vertical Devolution

→ Horizontal Devolution

→ Grants

📌 Must-Memorise

This is the core resource-sharing chain.

  • Specified duties.

  • Union levies.

  • Union levy and collection.
  • Union-State apportionment.

61. Article 270 Memory Chain

  • Shareable Union taxes.
  • Divisible pool.
  • Finance Commission.
  • Vertical + horizontal devolution.

62. Article 271 Memory Chain

  • Proceeds accrue to Union.

63. Grants Memory Chain

  • Article 275 → Grants-in-aid.
  • Article 282 → Public-purpose grants.
  • Finance Commission transfers ≠ All Union transfers.

64. Fiscal Imbalance Memory Chain

  • Vertical imbalance → Union vs States.
  • Horizontal imbalance → Differences among States.
  • Vertical remedy → Tax devolution + grants.
  • Horizontal remedy → Formula + equalisation.

65. GST Federalism Memory Chain

  • Article 246A → GST legislative power.
  • Article 269A → Inter-State GST.
  • Article 279A → GST Council.
  • Union vote → 1/3.
  • States → 2/3.
  • Decision → 3/4 weighted majority.

66. Divisible Pool Memory Chain

Gross Union Tax Revenue

↓

Remove Constitutional Exclusions / Relevant Adjustments

↓

Divisible Pool

41% to States Collectively

↓

Horizontal Distribution Among States

67. Sixteenth Finance Commission Memory Chain

  • Award → 2026–31.
  • States collectively → 41%.
  • Union → 59%.
  • Population → 17.5%.
  • Demographic Performance → 10%.
  • Area → 10%.
  • Forest → 10%.
  • GSDP Distance → 42.5%.
  • GDP Contribution → 10%.

68. Tamil Nadu Memory Chain

  • Tamil Nadu inter se share → 4.097%.
  • Applies within States' collective share.
  • Not a percentage of gross Union tax revenue.

  • Article 269 and Article 270 are different.
  • Divisible pool is not gross Union tax revenue.
  • Specific-purpose cesses are generally outside the ordinary divisible pool.
  • Article 271 surcharges accrue to the Union.
  • States' 41% share applies to the divisible pool.
  • Vertical devolution means Union vs States collectively.
  • Horizontal devolution means distribution among individual States.

  • Fiscal equalisation does not mean equal transfers.

  • GST Council represents cooperative fiscal federalism.
  • Union GST Council voting weight → 1/3.
  • States collectively → 2/3.

  • Cesses and surcharges are an important Centre-State fiscal debate.
  • Vertical fiscal imbalance concerns different levels of government.
  • Horizontal fiscal imbalance concerns differences among States.
  • Resource sharing must balance equity, performance, predictability and fiscal discipline.
